title: Lycaon
source: P. Ovidius Naso, Metamorphoses, ed. Hugo Magnus (Gotha: F.A. Perthes), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-latinLit phi0959.phi006.perseus-lat2, sha256 fb3fdb1d8a4a3b82. Collated against The Latin Library (cltk mirror) as a disagreement detector only. Original spelling kept. Pronunciation convention: reconstructed Classical (restored) Latin, applied consistently. All translations were made fresh from the Latin for Lectorium.
about: Jupiter, looking down from his citadel on the wickedness of the age, groans and calls the gods to council — and Ovid stages heaven as Rome: a road of great houses whose commons live elsewhere, a marble chamber, a presiding figure raised above the rest, and a quarter of the sky he dares to call the Palatine. To the assembled gods Jupiter explains why the human race must be destroyed: how, walking the earth in human shape, he came to the house of Lycaon, king of Arcadia, who mocked the signs of his divinity, plotted to kill him in his sleep, and then cut the throat of a hostage and served the half-living limbs at table, boiled and roasted. Jupiter burned the house down over it; Lycaon fled, tried to speak, and howled instead — and became the wolf whose nature he already had. The council roars its assent, then worries aloud about a world with no one left to carry incense to the altars, and is promised a new race of marvellous origin. The passage carries an open comparison between the shaken gods and Rome shaken by the assassination of Julius Caesar, and an address to Augustus by name. The killing, the cannibal meal and the physical detail of the transformation are set down plainly, and are translated here exactly as they stand.

sentences.t:
Quae pater ut summa vidit Saturnius arce,
ingemit et, facto nondum vulgata recenti,
foeda Lycaoniae referens convivia mensae,
ingentes animo et dignas Iove concipit iras,
sentences.l:
When these things the Saturnian father saw from his highest citadel,
he groans, and — not yet made public, the deed being fresh —
calling to mind the foul banqueting of Lycaon's table,
he conceives in his heart a rage enormous and worthy of Jove,
sentences.i: When the father, Saturn's son, saw all this from the height of his citadel, he groans; and calling to mind the foul feast at Lycaon's table — a thing not yet noised abroad, so fresh was the deed — he conceives in his heart a rage vast and worthy of Jove,
sentences.n: 'Quae' opens the sentence as a connecting relative — 'and these things', looking back to the wickedness just described. 'pater Saturnius' is the Saturnian father, Jupiter son of Saturn; Ovid names gods by their descent constantly. 'facto ... recenti' is an ablative absolute, 'the deed being fresh', explaining why the crime is 'nondum vulgata' (not yet spread abroad) — 'vulgata' is neuter plural, agreeing with 'convivia'. 'vidit' is perfect, but 'ingemit' and 'concipit' are present ('ingemuit' would be the perfect): the historic present takes over the moment the reaction begins. The adjectives 'ingentes ... dignas' are split far from their noun 'iras', which Ovid holds back to the end of the line.

sentences.t: conciliumque vocat: tenuit mora nulla vocatos.
sentences.l: and he calls a council: no delay held back those called.
sentences.n: 'concilium' is a formally summoned assembly, and 'vocare' is the verb used of a magistrate calling one: Jupiter summons the gods much as Rome's presiding magistrate summoned the senate, which is the picture the next lines build. 'vocat' beside 'concipit' keeps the historic present running. 'vocatos' is a perfect passive participle used as a noun, 'those who had been summoned' — the summons and the obedience land in the same half-line.

sentences.t:
Est via sublimis, caelo manifesta sereno:
lactea nomen habet, candore notabilis ipso.
Hac iter est superis ad magni tecta Tonantis
regalemque domum.
sentences.l:
There is a road on high, plain to see when the sky is clear:
Milky it has for a name, marked out by its very whiteness.
By this the gods above have their way to the halls of the great Thunderer
and his royal house.
sentences.i: There is a road on high, plain to see when the sky is clear; the Milky Way it is called, unmistakable for its very whiteness. By this road the gods pass to the halls of the great Thunderer and to his royal house.
sentences.n: 'lactea nomen habet' — 'it has Milky for a name': the Milky Way, 'via lactea'. 'caelo sereno' and 'candore ipso' are both bare ablatives — 'when the sky is clear', 'by its whiteness itself'. 'iter est superis' is a dative of possession, 'there is a road for the gods above' = 'the gods have a road'. 'Tonans', the Thunderer, is a cult title of Jupiter, and there was a temple of Iuppiter Tonans on the Capitol — the Roman overlay begins here.

sentences.t:
Dextra laevaque deorum
atria nobilium valvis celebrantur apertis
(plebs habitat diversa locis): hac parte potentes
caelicolae clarique suos posuere penates.
sentences.l:
On the right and on the left the halls of the noble gods
are thronged, their folding doors thrown open
(the commons live apart, in scattered quarters): in this quarter the powerful
and illustrious sky-dwellers have set up their own household gods.
sentences.i: To right and left stand the halls of the gods of rank, doors thrown wide and crowded with callers — the commons live elsewhere, in scattered quarters. Here in this precinct the powerful and illustrious dwellers in heaven have set up their household gods.
sentences.n: The whole picture is Rome: 'atria' with 'valvis apertis' that are 'celebrantur' (thronged) is precisely a great Roman house at the morning salutatio; 'plebs' is the Roman commons, housed away from the mansions; 'penates' are the household gods a family installs in its own home. 'valvis apertis' is an ablative absolute, 'with the doors standing open'. 'posuere' = 'posuerunt', the poetic third-plural perfect in '-ēre' — you will meet it on nearly every page of the poem. The gods are sorted here by rank and address, exactly as Romans were.

sentences.t:
Hic locus est, quem, si verbis audacia detur,
haud timeam magni dixisse Palatia caeli.
sentences.l:
This is the place which — if boldness were granted to my words —
I should not fear to have called the Palatine of great heaven.
sentences.n: 'si ... detur ... haud timeam' is the future-less-vivid condition, both verbs present subjunctive: 'if boldness should be granted ... I should not fear'. 'dixisse' is a perfect infinitive where English wants a present one ('to call'), a common licence in verse. The Palatine was the hill where Augustus lived; naming heaven's high quarter after it is what the whole description has been building toward, and Ovid marks his own nerve in the word 'audacia'.

sentences.t:
Ergo ubi marmoreo superi sedere recessu,
celsior ipse loco sceptroque innixus eburno
terrificam capitis concussit terque quaterque
caesariem, cum qua terram, mare, sidera movit.
sentences.l:
So, when the gods above had taken their seats in the marble recess,
he himself, higher by his place and leaning on his ivory sceptre,
shook three times and four the terrifying
hair of his head — and with it he moved earth, sea and stars.
sentences.i: So, when the gods had taken their seats in the marble chamber, he himself — raised above them by his place, leaning on his ivory sceptre — shook three times and four the dreadful mane of his head, and with it moved earth and sea and stars.
sentences.n: 'sedere' = 'sedērunt', the '-ēre' perfect again. 'celsior loco' is an ablative of respect, 'higher in respect of his seat' — the raised chair of a presiding magistrate. The adjective 'terrificam' is stranded at one line's end and its noun 'caesariem' opens the next, so the image lands late and heavily. 'cum qua' is an ordinary relative reaching back to 'caesariem' — 'with which', which English turns into 'and with it'; the ivory sceptre belongs to the Roman world of consuls and triumphs as much as to Olympus.

sentences.t: Talibus inde modis ora indignantia solvit:
sentences.l: Then in words like these he unloosed his indignant lips:
sentences.n: 'ora solvere' — 'to loose the mouth' — is the epic formula for beginning to speak. 'indignantia' is a present participle agreeing with 'ora': it is the lips themselves that are indignant, the feeling handed over to the part of the body that shows it.

sentences.t:
“Non ego pro mundi regno magis anxius illa
tempestate fui, qua centum quisque parabat
inicere anguipedum captivo bracchia caelo.
sentences.l:
'Not more anxious was I for the sovereignty of the world at that
time when each of the snake-footed ones was making ready
to throw a hundred arms upon a captive heaven.
sentences.i: 'I was in no greater dread for my rule over the world in that hour when each of the snake-footed giants was making ready to fling a hundred arms about a captive heaven.
sentences.n: 'tempestate' carries its older sense here, 'time, season', not 'storm' — 'illa tempestate', 'at that time'. 'anguipedum' ('of the snake-footed') is the Giants, who piled mountain on mountain to storm the sky; 'captivo caelo' is dative with 'inicere' and treats heaven as already a prisoner. Jupiter opens by measuring the present crisis against the worst thing that ever befell him.

sentences.t:
Nam quamquam ferus hostis erat, tamen illud ab uno
corpore et ex una pendebat origine bellum.
sentences.l:
For although the enemy was savage, still that war
hung from a single body and from a single source.
sentences.i: For savage though that enemy was, the war still hung upon one stock and sprang from a single origin.
sentences.n: 'quamquam ... tamen' — 'although ... nevertheless' — with the indicative, since the concession is a fact. 'illud ... bellum' is pulled wide apart around the line-end, its noun arriving only at the close: the war was one thing, as the phrase finally proves to be one phrase. 'ab uno corpore' = from one body, one stock of enemies; the present threat, by contrast, is everywhere at once.

sentences.t:
Nunc mihi, qua totum Nereus circumsonat orbem,
perdendum est mortale genus: per flumina iuro
infera, sub terras Stygio labentia luco!
sentences.l:
Now the mortal race must be destroyed by me, wherever
Nereus sounds about the whole globe: I swear by the rivers
below, gliding beneath the earth through the Stygian grove!
sentences.i: Now the mortal race must be destroyed by me, everywhere the sea roars round the globe. I swear it by the rivers of the world below, that glide beneath the earth through the grove of Styx!
sentences.n: 'mihi ... perdendum est' is the passive periphrastic with dative of agent — 'it must be destroyed by me' — the flat grammar of an obligation already settled. 'Nereus', the old sea-god, stands for the sea itself. The oath by the infernal rivers is the one oath no god may break, so Jupiter closes the question before the council can open it.

sentences.t:
cuncta prius temptata: sed inmedicabile corpus
ense recidendum est, ne pars sincera trahatur.
sentences.l:
All has been tried before: but the body past curing
must be cut away with the blade, lest the sound part be drawn in.
sentences.i: Everything else has been tried already; but flesh past curing must be cut away with the blade, before the healthy part is drawn into the infection too.
sentences.n: 'temptata' has its 'sunt' left out, as Latin freely leaves it out; 'recidendum est' is the passive periphrastic once more. 'ne ... trahatur' is a negative purpose clause, 'so that the sound part may not be dragged in'. The edition prints 'temptata' where some editions print 'temptanda' — settled fact ('all has been tried') against a duty still ahead ('all must be tried first'). The surgeon's knife is the whole justification for the flood to come.

sentences.t:
Sunt mihi semidei, sunt rustica numina, nymphae
faunique satyrique et monticolae silvani:
sentences.l:
There are to me demigods, there are rustic powers — nymphs
and fauns and satyrs and the mountain-haunting woodland spirits:
sentences.i: I have demigods; I have the powers of the countryside — nymphs, fauns, satyrs, and the silvans who haunt the hills.
sentences.n: 'sunt mihi' is the dative of possession, 'there are to me' = 'I have', the ordinary Latin way of saying it. The doubled '-que ... -que' of 'faunique satyrique' is an epic mannerism that piles the names up. These are the lesser powers of field and hill. Heaven sorts its ranks exactly as the houses were sorted at line 173 — except that these do not live in heaven at all, as the next line says outright.

sentences.t:
quos quoniam caeli nondum dignamur honore,
quas dedimus certe terras habitare sinamus.
sentences.l:
and since we do not yet deem them worthy of heaven's honour,
let us at least allow them to dwell in the lands we have given them.
sentences.n: 'quos' opens as a connecting relative, 'and them'. 'dignamur' is deponent and takes the ablative 'honore', 'we deem worthy of the honour'; the first-person plurals here are Jupiter's royal 'we'. 'sinamus' is hortatory subjunctive, 'let us allow'. Notice 'quas dedimus certe terras': the antecedent 'terras' has been drawn inside its own relative clause and stands after the verb, which Latin does freely and English simply cannot.

sentences.t:
An satis, o superi, tutos fore creditis illos,
cum mihi, qui fulmen, qui vos habeoque regoque,
struxerit insidias notus feritate Lycaon?”
sentences.l:
Or do you believe, gods above, that they will be safe enough,
when against me — I who hold and rule the thunderbolt, and you —
Lycaon, notorious for savagery, has laid an ambush?'
sentences.i: Or do you truly believe they will be safe, when against me — who hold and govern the thunderbolt, and you as well — Lycaon, a byword for savagery, has laid his plot?'
sentences.n: 'tutos fore' is indirect statement after 'creditis': accusative with infinitive, 'fore' being the future infinitive of 'sum', 'will be'. 'qui ... habeoque regoque' keeps first-person verbs after the relative because Jupiter is his own antecedent — 'I, who hold ...'. 'cum ... struxerit' (cum with perfect subjunctive) gives the grounds, 'seeing that he has laid'. Lycaon's name is held back to the very last word of the speech.

sentences.t:
Confremuere omnes studiisque ardentibus ausum
talia deposcunt.
sentences.l:
All roared together, and with burning zeal
they demand the one who had dared such things.
sentences.i: A roar went up from all of them, and in blazing eagerness they demand the man who had dared such a thing.
sentences.n: 'Confremuere' = 'confremuerunt' — the '-ēre' perfect once more. 'ausum' is the perfect participle of the deponent 'audeo' used as a noun, 'the one having dared'; deponent participles are active in sense. 'deposcunt' is the technical word for demanding that a man be handed over for punishment — the shout of a Roman senate, not of an Olympian chorus.

sentences.t:
Sic, cum manus inpia saevit
sanguine Caesareo Romanum exstinguere nomen,
attonitum tanto subitae terrore ruinae
humanum genus est totusque perhorruit orbis:
sentences.l:
Just so, when an impious band raged to blot out
the Roman name in Caesar's blood,
the human race was stunned with so great a terror at the sudden
downfall, and the whole world shuddered:
sentences.i: So it was when an unholy gang raged to put out the name of Rome in Caesar's blood: mankind stood stunned in terror at that sudden ruin, and the whole world shuddered.
sentences.n: The simile steps out of myth into living memory: the assassination of Julius Caesar in 44 BC. 'saevit ... exstinguere' — 'raged to blot out' — is a poetic infinitive of purpose after a verb that does not normally govern one. 'tanto subitae terrore ruinae' interlocks two noun-and-adjective pairs ('so great a terror', 'the sudden downfall'), an arrangement Latin verse loves and English can only unpick. On the tenses: 'saevit' may be read as present, holding the crime before the eye, or as the contracted perfect 'saeviit'; the world's answer is plainly perfect, 'attonitum est ... perhorruit'.

sentences.t:
nec tibi grata minus pietas, Auguste, tuorum est,
quam fuit illa Iovi. Qui postquam voce manuque
murmura conpressit, tenuere silentia cuncti.
sentences.l:
nor is the devotion of your own people less welcome to you, Augustus,
than that was to Jove. And when he with voice and hand
had checked the murmuring, all held their silence.
sentences.i: and the loyalty of your own people is no less welcome to you, Augustus, than theirs was to Jove. And when he had checked the murmuring with voice and hand, they all kept silence.
sentences.n: Ovid turns from the story to address the emperor directly — apostrophe, 'tibi ... Auguste' — and the proportion is exact: the gods stand to Jupiter as Rome's loyal citizens stand to Augustus. 'pietas' is not piety in the churchly sense but the loyalty owed to gods, country and kin. 'Qui' is a connecting relative, 'and he'. 'tenuere' = 'tenuerunt', with plural 'silentia' where English says 'silence'.

sentences.t:
Substitit ut clamor pressus gravitate regentis,
Iuppiter hoc iterum sermone silentia rupit:
sentences.l:
When the shouting had stopped, checked by the weight of their ruler,
Jupiter broke the silence again with this speech:
sentences.n: 'ut' with the perfect indicative means 'when, as soon as' — not 'in order that'; the mood tells you which it is. 'gravitate regentis' — 'by the weight of the one ruling': 'gravitas' is the Roman name for the moral authority a presiding man carries, and 'regentis' is a participle standing as a noun. 'silentia rupit', plural again for a single hush.

sentences.t:
“Ille quidem poenas, curam hanc dimittite, solvit.
Quod tamen admissum, quae sit vindicta, docebo.
sentences.l:
'He, at any rate, has paid the penalty — let that care go.
But what the offence was, and what the vengeance is, I shall tell you.
sentences.n: 'curam hanc dimittite' is an imperative dropped bodily inside the sentence, cutting across it: 'let this worry go'. 'Quod ... admissum (sit), quae sit vindicta' are indirect questions, which is why the verbs stand in the subjunctive — a 'what', 'who' or 'why' clause depending on a verb of telling or asking always takes it. 'admissum' is a participle used as a noun, 'a thing committed', an offence.

sentences.i: The evil report of the age had reached my ears; longing to find it false, I glide down from the height of Olympus and, god that I am, walk the earth in human form.
sentences.n: 'quam' is a connecting relative picking up 'infamia' — 'and this, wishing it false'; 'cupiens falsam' leaves out 'esse', as Latin regularly does. 'delabor' and 'lustro' switch to the present after the pluperfect 'contigerat': the historic present, which brings the story up close. 'nostras ... aures' is the royal plural, like 'dignamur' and 'dedimus' earlier in the speech. 'deus' sits in apposition to the 'I' of 'lustro' — 'I, a god' — set pointedly beside 'humana ... imagine'.

sentences.t:
Longa mora est, quantum noxae sit ubique repertum,
enumerare: minor fuit ipsa infamia vero.
sentences.l:
It is a long business to count up how much wickedness
was found everywhere: the ill fame itself was less than the truth.
sentences.i: It would take too long to reckon up how much guilt was to be found in every place; the report itself fell short of the truth.
sentences.n: 'Longa mora est ... enumerare' — 'to count them up is a long delay', with the infinitive standing as the subject of 'est'. 'quantum noxae' is a partitive genitive, 'how much of wickedness'; being an indirect question it puts 'sit repertum' in the subjunctive. 'vero' is an ablative of comparison after 'minor', 'less than the truth'.

sentences.t:
Maenala transieram latebris horrenda ferarum
et cum Cyllene gelidi pineta Lycaei:
Arcadis hinc sedes et inhospita tecta tyranni
ingredior, traherent cum sera crepuscula noctem.
sentences.l:
I had crossed Maenalus, dreadful with the lairs of wild beasts,
and, with Cyllene, the pinewoods of cold Lycaeus:
from there I enter the seat and the inhospitable roof of the Arcadian
tyrant, at the hour when late dusk was drawing night on.
sentences.i: I had crossed Maenalus, a place of dread for its dens of wild beasts, and Cyllene too, and the pine woods of cold Lycaeus; from there I enter the dwelling and the unwelcoming house of the Arcadian tyrant, at the hour when late dusk was drawing the night on behind it.
sentences.n: The three names are Arcadian mountains — Maenalus, Cyllene, Lycaeus — and Lycaeus is not idle: the mountain, and the Zeus worshipped on it, carry the wolf ('lykos' in Greek) into the story before Lycaon is even named. 'inhospita tecta' lays the charge in advance: the crime will be a breach of hospitality, the one thing a wandering god exists to test. 'traherent cum ... crepuscula' is cum with the imperfect subjunctive for attendant circumstance, 'at the time when dusk was drawing'. 'ingredior' is deponent and present — the historic present again.

sentences.t:
Signa dedi venisse deum, vulgusque precari
coeperat: inridet primo pia vota Lycaon,
mox ait
sentences.l:
I gave signs that a god had come, and the crowd had begun
to pray: at first Lycaon laughs at their pious vows,
then he says
sentences.n: 'signa dedi venisse deum' — 'I gave signs (that) a god had come': the accusative-and-infinitive of indirect statement hangs on 'signa dedi' as though it were a verb of saying. Pluperfect 'coeperat' then present 'inridet ... ait' — the tense drops into the historic present exactly where the scene turns. 'pia vota' are the prayers of proper reverence, and Lycaon's laugh at them is his first offence, before he lifts a knife.

sentences.t:
”experiar deus hic, discrimine aperto,
an sit mortalis. Nec erit dubitabile verum.”
sentences.l:
"I will find out, by a test laid open,
whether this one is a god or mortal. And the truth will not be doubtful."
sentences.i: "By a test that leaves nothing hidden I shall find out whether this is a god or a mortal. And the truth will not be in question."
sentences.n: An alternative indirect question: 'deus hic ... an sit mortalis', 'whether this one is a god ... or mortal' — the first limb goes without a particle, and 'sit' is subjunctive because the question is reported. 'hic' is best taken as the demonstrative, 'this fellow', the subject of 'sit', rather than the adverb 'here'. 'discrimine aperto' is an ablative absolute, 'the trial being laid open'; 'discrimen' is the decisive point at which a thing is settled either way. Lycaon proposes to settle godhead by experiment, and that is the impiety exactly.

sentences.t:
Nocte gravem somno necopina perdere morte
me parat: haec illi placet experientia veri.
sentences.l:
By night, as I lay heavy with sleep, to destroy me by an unlooked-for
death he makes ready: this is the test of truth that pleases him.
sentences.i: By night, while I lay heavy with sleep, he makes ready to do away with me by an unlooked-for death: that is the trial of the truth that suits him.
sentences.n: The words are woven so that victim and killing are tangled together — 'gravem somno' (me, heavy with sleep) and 'necopina ... morte' (by an unforeseen death) interlock, and the governing 'me parat' only lands at the start of the next line. 'experientia veri' picks up his own boast 'experiar': his idea of an experiment is murder.

sentences.t:
Nec contentus eo est: missi de gente Molossa
obsidis unius iugulum mucrone resolvit,
sentences.l:
Nor is he content with that: of a single hostage sent
from the Molossian nation he unlooses the throat with the sword's point,
sentences.i: Nor is that enough for him: with a sword he opens the throat of one of the hostages sent from the Molossian people,
sentences.n: 'resolvit' means literally 'unfastens, unties', and 'mucro' is the point of the blade, not the blade at large; used of a throat the phrase is cold understatement. The long genitive phrase 'missi de gente Molossa obsidis unius' wraps across the line-break before the noun it depends on, 'iugulum', finally arrives. A hostage was a pledge of good faith and stood under his host's protection, so this is a second breach of the very duty Lycaon has already broken toward his guest; the Molossians were a people of Epirus, best known for their dogs.

sentences.t:
atque ita semineces partim ferventibus artus
mollit aquis, partim subiecto torruit igni.
sentences.l:
and then the still half-living limbs he softens, part of them,
in boiling water, part he roasted over fire set beneath.
sentences.i: and then the limbs, still half alive, he softens — some of them in boiling water, some he roasted over a fire laid underneath.
sentences.n: 'semineces' — 'half-dead' — is split from its noun 'artus' and thrown to the front of the clause: the limbs are still twitching when they go into the water. 'partim ... partim' = 'partly ... partly'. Present 'mollit' beside perfect 'torruit' in one sentence is Ovid's usual alternation, holding one action open and closing the other. The verbs are the ordinary words of a kitchen, which is what makes the line horrible.

sentences.t:
Quod simul inposuit mensis, ego vindice flamma
in domino dignos everti tecta penates.
sentences.l:
And as soon as he had set this on the table, I with avenging flame
brought the roof down upon household gods worthy of their master.
sentences.i: And the moment he set it on the tables, I brought the roof down with avenging fire upon household gods well worthy of their master.
sentences.n: 'Quod' is a connecting relative — 'and this', the dish. 'simul' here stands for 'simul ac', 'as soon as'. 'in ... penates' is 'down onto the household gods', and 'domino dignos' ('worthy of their master') is bitter: the gods of that house had earned what fell on them. 'vindice flamma' is an ablative of means with 'vindex' pressed into service as an adjective, 'with avenging flame'.

sentences.t:
Territus ipse fugit, nactusque silentia ruris
exululat frustraque loqui conatur:
sentences.l:
Terrified, he himself flees, and having gained the silence of the countryside
he howls aloud and tries in vain to speak:
sentences.n: 'nactus' is the perfect participle of the deponent 'nanciscor' (light upon, come by) and is active in sense — 'having reached'. 'exululat' is built on the howl itself ('ululare') and is the first thing in him to change: the voice goes before the body does.

sentences.t:
ab ipso
conligit os rabiem, solitaeque cupidine caedis
vertitur in pecudes et nunc quoque sanguine gaudet.
sentences.l:
from his own self
his mouth gathers its madness, and out of craving for his accustomed slaughter
he turns against the flocks, and even now he delights in blood.
sentences.i: his jaws take their rabid fury from the man himself; and with the old craving for slaughter he turns on the flocks, and even now he takes joy in blood.
sentences.n: 'ab ipso ... os rabiem' — the madness of the wolf's jaws comes 'from the man himself': the beast is not something added to him, it is what he already was. 'solitae ... caedis' is an objective genitive after 'cupidine', 'a craving for his accustomed killing'. 'nunc quoque' is the plain adverb, 'even now', and it opens the tale out of the past into the wolf that still exists — though watch elsewhere for 'quoque' that is really 'quō-que', 'and by which'.

sentences.t:
In villos abeunt vestes, in crura lacerti:
fit lupus et veteris servat vestigia formae.
sentences.l:
His clothes pass away into shaggy hair, his arms into legs:
he becomes a wolf, and keeps the traces of his former shape.
sentences.n: 'in ... abeunt' — 'they go away into' — is one of Ovid's standing formulas for a body becoming something else, and it recurs through the poem. The second half of the line drops the verb altogether ('in crura lacerti', 'his arms into legs'), so the change outruns the grammar. And it is not an erasure: 'servat vestigia', the old shape stays legible in the new one.

sentences.t:
Canities eadem est, eadem violentia vultus,
idem oculi lucent, eadem feritatis imago est.
sentences.l:
The grey of his hair is the same, the same the violence of his face,
the same eyes gleam, the same is the look of savagery.
sentences.i: The same grey hair, the same violence in the face; the same eyes glare; savagery wears the same look as before.
sentences.n: Four clauses, and 'eadem ... eadem ... idem ... eadem' opens or dominates each of them — anaphora, hammering the sameness home. Three drop the verb entirely; only 'lucent' is spoken aloud. 'canities' is the grey or white of age, and it belonged to the man before it belonged to the wolf.

sentences.t:
Occidit una domus. Sed non domus una perire
digna fuit: qua terra patet, fera regnat Erinys.
sentences.l:
One house has fallen. But not one house alone was deserving
to perish: as far as earth lies open, the savage Fury reigns.
sentences.i: One house has fallen — but it was not one house alone that deserved to perish. As far as the earth reaches, the savage Fury holds sway.
sentences.n: 'una domus' is repeated in successive lines with the sense turned inside out — one house fell, one house was not enough. 'digna fuit' takes the infinitive 'perire', 'deserved to perish'. 'qua terra patet' — 'where the earth lies open', i.e. everywhere. An 'Erinys' is a Fury, one of the avenging spirits of blood-guilt; Jupiter enlarges one man's crime into a condition of the whole world, which is the step that licenses the flood.

sentences.t:
In facinus iurasse putes. Dent ocius omnes
quas meruere pati (sic stat sententia) poenas.”
sentences.l:
You would think they had sworn an oath into crime. Let them all pay,
and quickly, the penalties they have earned to suffer — so stands the sentence.'
sentences.i: You would think they had all sworn a common oath to wickedness. Let them all pay, and quickly, the penalties they have deserved to suffer — so my sentence stands.'
sentences.n: 'putes' is the potential subjunctive, 'you would think' — the indefinite second person, anyone who looked. 'in facinus iurasse' uses the idiom of swearing an oath to a thing ('iurare in verba', to swear to another man's words), here 'sworn into a crime'; 'iurasse' is the shortened form of 'iuravisse'. 'Dent' is jussive, 'let them give (pay)'. 'meruere' = 'meruerunt', the '-ēre' perfect; and 'quas ... poenas' wraps the whole clause, parenthesis and all, before its noun arrives at the very last word.

sentences.t:
Dicta Iovis pars voce probant stimulosque frementi
adiciunt, alii partes adsensibus inplent.
sentences.l:
Jove's words a part approve aloud, and to him as he rages
they add goads; the others fill out their parts with assent.
sentences.i: Some approve Jove's words aloud and spur him on as he storms; the rest play out their parts with murmurs of assent.
sentences.n: 'pars ... probant' takes a plural verb although 'pars' is singular — construction according to sense, normal with collective nouns. 'stimulos adiciunt frementi' — 'they add goads to him as he rages': 'frementi' is a dative participle used as a noun, and a 'stimulus' is the goad of a driver. 'partes ... inplent' is stage language, to fill out one's role — the council is playing a scene, and Ovid lets the word say so.

sentences.t:
Est tamen humani generis iactura dolori
omnibus, et, quae sit terrae mortalibus orbae
forma futura, rogant, quis sit laturus in aras
tura, ferisne paret populandas tradere terras.
sentences.l:
Yet the loss of the human race is a grief to them all,
and they ask what shape the earth is going to have
when it is bereft of mortals, who will bring incense to the altars,
whether he means to hand the lands over to wild beasts to be laid waste.
sentences.i: Yet the loss of the human race is a grief to them all, and they ask what the earth is to look like once it is emptied of mortals; who will carry incense to the altars; whether he means to hand the lands over to the beasts to be laid waste.
sentences.n: 'iactura ... dolori omnibus (est)' is the double dative: a thing 'is for a grief to' someone — predicative dative 'dolori' with dative of the person 'omnibus'. Three indirect questions follow in a row ('quae sit ... forma futura', 'quis sit laturus', 'ferisne paret'), all with subjunctive verbs; the '-ne' fastened to 'feris' asks 'whether'. 'populandas ... terras' is a gerundive after 'tradere', 'the lands to be laid waste'. 'terrae ... orbae' is 'the earth bereft of', with 'orbus' taking the ablative 'mortalibus' — and the gods' worry is frankly self-interested: no mortals, no incense.

sentences.t:
Talia quaerentes (sibi enim fore cetera curae)
rex superum trepidare vetat subolemque priori
dissimilem populo promittit origine mira.
sentences.l:
As they ask such things — for the rest, he said, would be his own care —
the king of the gods above forbids them to be alarmed, and a stock unlike
the former people he promises, of marvellous origin.
sentences.i: While they ask such things — the rest, he tells them, would be his own concern — the king of the gods forbids them to be alarmed, and promises a race unlike the people before it, sprung from a marvellous beginning.
sentences.n: 'sibi ... fore cetera curae' is indirect statement with the double dative again — 'that the rest would be for a care to him' — reporting what Jupiter says with no verb of saying anywhere in sight; 'fore' is the future infinitive of 'sum'. 'trepidare vetat' takes a bare infinitive, 'forbids (them) to be alarmed'. 'subolem ... priori dissimilem populo' — 'a stock unlike the former people' — goes unexplained here, and the part closes on 'origine mira', a marvellous origin still withheld.

glossary.vero: vērum — the truth (n. abl. of comparison after 'minor')
